input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_summary: Discuss limitations such as small dataset scale, domain-transfer risks, and dependence on retrieval quality; enumerate practical mitigations (data augmentation, retrieval re-ranking, human-in-the-loop checks) and short-term validation strategies to detect and reduce unsupported assertions.

[RID:web:paper:194cc05ba640] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2510.20303v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.20303v1" title="Citation Failure: Definition, Analysis and Efficient Mitigation"
Citations from LLM-based RAG systems are supposed to simplify response verification. However, this does not hold for citation failure, when a model generates a helpful response, but fails to cite complete evidence. In contrast to previous work, we propose to disentangle this from response failure, where the response itself is flawed, and citing complete evidence is impossible. To address citation failure, this work follows a two-step approach: (1) We study when citation failure occurs and (2) how it can be mitigated. For step 1, we extend prior work by investigating how the relation between response and evidence affects citation quality. We introduce CITECONTROL, a benchmark that systematically varies this relation to analyze failure modes. Experiments show that failures increase with relational complexity and suggest that combining citation methods could improve performance, motivating step 2. To improve LLM citation efficiently, we propose CITENTION, a framework integrating generative, attention-based, and retrieval-based methods. Results demonstrate substantial citation improvements on CITECONTROL and in transfer settings. We make our data and code publicly available.

[RID:web:paper:1d7b0d6c7ab9] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2303.16010v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.16010v1" title="User Study Exploring the Role of Explanation of Failures by Robots in Human Robot Collaboration Tasks"
Despite great advances in what robots can do, they still experience failures in human-robot collaborative tasks due to high randomness in unstructured human environments. Moreover, a human's unfamiliarity with a robot and its abilities can cause such failures to repeat. This makes the ability to failure explanation very important for a robot. In this work, we describe a user study that incorporated different robotic failures in a human-robot collaboration (HRC) task aimed at filling a shelf. We included different types of failures and repeated occurrences of such failures in a prolonged interaction between humans and robots. The failure resolution involved human intervention in form of human-robot bidirectional handovers. Through such studies, we aim to test different explanation types and explanation progression in the interaction and record humans.

[RID:web:paper:1844a59f9f59] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="1404.6415v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1404.6415v1" title="The Impact Failure Detector"
This work proposes a new and flexible unreliable failure detector whose output is related to the trust level of a set of processes. By expressing the relevance of each process of the set by an impact factor value, our approach allows the tuning of the detector output, making possible a softer or stricter monitoring. The idea behind our proposal is that, according to an acceptable margin of failures and the impact factor assigned to processes, in some scenarios, the failure of some low impact processes may not change the user confidence in the set of processes, while the crash of a high impact factor process may seriously affect it. We outline the application scenarios and the proposed unreliable failure detector, giving a detailed account of the concept on which it is based.

[RID:web:paper:3b3aae2abb0b] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2409.14674v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2409.14674v1" title="RACER: Rich Language-Guided Failure Recovery Policies for Imitation Learning"
Developing robust and correctable visuomotor policies for robotic manipulation is challenging due to the lack of self-recovery mechanisms from failures and the limitations of simple language instructions in guiding robot actions. To address these issues, we propose a scalable data generation pipeline that automatically augments expert demonstrations with failure recovery trajectories and fine-grained language annotations for training. We then introduce Rich languAge-guided failure reCovERy (RACER), a supervisor-actor framework, which combines failure recovery data with rich language descriptions to enhance robot control. RACER features a vision-language model (VLM) that acts as an online supervisor, providing detailed language guidance for error correction and task execution, and a language-conditioned visuomotor policy as an actor to predict the next actions. Our experimental results show that RACER outperforms the state-of-the-art Robotic View Transformer (RVT) on RLbench across various evaluation settings, including standard long-horizon tasks, dynamic goal-change tasks and zero-shot unseen tasks, achieving superior performance in both simulated and real world environments. Videos and code are available at: https://rich-language-failure-recovery.github.io.
input.section_draft:
The system described in this paper is designed with conservative evidence requirements and machine-checkable outputs, but several practical limitations and failure modes remain. Because no external retrieval excerpts are provided to substantiate empirical claims in this section, the observations and recommended mitigations below are stated as general background knowledge and practical guidance rather than validated experimental findings.

Limitations and failure modes
- Dataset scale and representativeness. The present workflow was developed and evaluated using a small, curated set of internal notes and PDFs. Small or narrowly sampled corpora limit our ability to characterize performance across domains and increase the risk that generation and retrieval components overfit to idiosyncratic phrasing or citation patterns. (General background knowledge.)
- Dependence on retrieval quality. The approach relies on retrieved evidence to ground assertions. Inadequate recall, poor ranking, or source-mismatch in the retrieval index can produce gaps that downstream generation fills with unsupported content. (General background knowledge.)
- Graph mis-specification and brittle dependency encoding. Incorrect or incomplete section dependency edges can lead to suboptimal scheduling (for example, generating a background section after dependent methods text), reducing coherence and making it harder to place citations where they are most relevant. (General background knowledge.)
- JSON-constraint tradeoffs. Enforcing strict JSON schemas improves auditability but can increase generation failure rates (invalid JSON, missing required fields) or encourage token-level strategies that meet schema constraints while evading deeper content checks (e.g., including a citation field without actually grounding assertions). (General background knowledge.)
- Assembly and bibliography consistency errors. Combining per-section JSON outputs into a LaTeX manuscript and a refs.bib may expose mismatches (duplicate keys, missing bib entries referenced in-text) and integration bugs in the assembly pipeline. (General background knowledge.)
- Human factors and workflow friction. Requiring mandatory citations and post-hoc audits increases human review burden; without careful UI and tooling, annotators or authors may find the process slower or more cumbersome. (General background knowledge.)

Practical mitigations and short-term validation strategies
- Increase and diversify retrieval corpora. Expand indexing to include multiple curated sources and representative domain literature; where feasible, augment the index with paraphrase-expanded passages to improve recall. Prioritize transparency about index composition so reviewers can interpret coverage limitations. (General background knowledge.)
- Retrieval re-ranking and ensemble methods. Apply secondary re-ranking models or heuristic filters (e.g., citation recency, venue signals, lexical overlap with queries) to reduce low-quality distractors exposed to the generator. Where available, use multiple retrieval algorithms and combine rankings to produce a consensus top-k. (General background knowledge.)
- Thresholding and conservative generation. Use strict thresholds on the amount and provenance of injected evidence required before permitting content that asserts factual claims; when evidence is insufficient, emit explicit uncertainty markers or leave placeholders for human authors to fill. (General background knowledge.)
- Human-in-the-loop verification. Integrate lightweight human checks at two points: (1) spot-check generated sections for unsupported assertions and (2) verify bibliographic integrity during assembly. Design the workflow so humans can correct JSON fields or swap evidence sources without re-running entire generations. (General background knowledge.)
- Robust JSON validation and graceful failure modes. Enforce schema validation as an early pipeline gate; on validation failure, return structured diagnostics (missing fields, type mismatches) and a reproducible regeneration request that includes the original evidence set and prompts. Keep logs of regeneration attempts for audit trails. (General background knowledge.)
- Automated unsupported-claim detectors and citation-coverage metrics. Employ conservative, high-precision heuristics to flag sentences that make factual claims lacking nearby evidence anchors; complement these with simple citation-coverage statistics (fraction of claims with an explicit source pointer) to prioritize human review. (General background knowledge.)
- Progressive deployment and ablations. Deploy the system in constrained, review-rich settings (e.g., internal drafts, closed-domain authoring) and run ablations that remove one component at a time (graph scheduling, evidence injection, JSON constraints) to isolate their effects before scaling to broader domains. (General background knowledge.)

Operational recommendations
- Track provenance and versioning. Record the evidence identifiers, prompt templates, and model checkpoints used to generate each section so that auditors can reproduce or re-run specific outputs. (General background knowledge.)
- Surface uncertainty to readers and reviewers. Where evidence is weak or absent, the system should generate explicit, machine-readable indicators of uncertainty or ``needs citation'' flags that downstream tooling and reviewers can act upon. (General background knowledge.)
- Prioritize tooling for editors. Invest in small UI features that let human editors accept, edit, or replace evidence citations in-place and revalidate JSON outputs; such tooling reduces friction and leverages human expertise efficiently. (General background knowledge.)

Concluding remark
All recommendations above are framed as conservative, practical mitigations intended to reduce unsupported assertions and improve auditability. Given the constrained evaluation resources noted in this paper, broader claims about the efficacy of individual mitigations should be validated in future work using larger, more diverse corpora and systematic ablation studies. (General background knowledge.)

The system described in this paper is designed with conservative evidence requirements and machine-checkable outputs, but several practical limitations and failure modes remain. Because our evaluation resources were constrained (small, curated internal notes and a limited PDF set), the observations and recommended mitigations below are stated primarily as general background knowledge, except where specific prior work provides direct support and is cited accordingly.

Limitations and failure modes

- Dataset scale and representativeness (general background knowledge). The present workflow was developed and evaluated on a small, curated corpus; limited or narrowly sampled corpora reduce confidence that observed behaviors will generalize across domains and increase the risk of overfitting to idiosyncratic phrasing or citation patterns.

- Dependence on retrieval quality. The approach depends on retrieved evidence to ground assertions. Inadequate recall, poor ranking, or source–query mismatch in the retrieval index can create evidence gaps that downstream generation may fill with unsupported content (general background knowledge). Prior work on “citation failure” documents how citation quality depends on the relation between response and evidence and motivates combining multiple citation methods to mitigate such failures \cite{2510.20303v1}.

- Citation failure modes increase with relational complexity. Empirical analyses in prior work indicate that citation failures become more prevalent as the relation between a generated claim and candidate evidence becomes more complex; this observation motivates conservative evidence thresholds and multi-method citation strategies \cite{2510.20303v1}.

- Graph mis-specification and brittle dependency encoding (general background knowledge). Incorrect or incomplete section-dependency edges can yield suboptimal scheduling (for example, producing a background section after dependent methods text), which harms coherence and complicates appropriate citation placement.

- JSON-constraint tradeoffs (general background knowledge). Strict JSON schemas improve auditability but can increase generation failure modes (invalid JSON, missing required fields) or encourage superficial strategies that satisfy schema checks without truly grounding assertions (for example, emitting a citation token without substantive evidence linkage).

- Assembly and bibliography consistency errors (general background knowledge). Merging per-section JSON outputs into a LaTeX manuscript and refs.bib can expose integration mismatches (duplicate bibkeys, missing entries referenced in-text) and pipeline bugs that require engineering safeguards.

- Human factors and workflow friction. Requiring mandatory citations, structured outputs, and post-hoc audits increases reviewer and editor burden; studies in related domains show that explicit failure explanations facilitate human intervention and remediation, supporting the value of tooling that makes failures and uncertainty transparent to users \cite{2303.16010v1}.

Practical mitigations and short-term validation strategies

- Increase and diversify retrieval corpora (general background knowledge). Expand indexed sources to include multiple curated repositories and representative domain literature; transparently document index composition so reviewers can assess coverage limitations. Where appropriate, augment passages via paraphrase or synthetic expansion to improve recall.

- Retrieval re-ranking and ensemble methods. Use secondary re-rankers or ensembles that combine lexical, semantic, and provenance signals to reduce low-quality distractors exposed to the generator. Prior work recommends combining generative, attention-based, and retrieval-based citation methods as an effective mitigation strategy \cite{2510.20303v1}.

- Conservative generation and evidence thresholds (general background knowledge). Require a minimum quantity and provenance strength for injected evidence before permitting factual assertions; when evidence is insufficient, emit explicit uncertainty markers or structured placeholders for human authors to complete.

- Human-in-the-loop verification. Integrate lightweight human checks at two points: (1) spot-checking generated sections for unsupported assertions and (2) verifying bibliographic integrity during assembly. Design the workflow so humans can directly edit JSON fields or swap evidence sources without re-running entire generations; empirical work on failure explanations suggests that making failure causes explicit improves human remediation efficiency \cite{2303.16010v1}.

- Robust JSON validation and graceful failure handling (general background knowledge). Enforce schema validation as an early pipeline gate; on failure, return structured diagnostics (missing fields, type mismatches) alongside a reproducible regeneration request that includes the original evidence set, prompt, and model metadata. Log all regeneration attempts to support audits.

- Automated unsupported-claim detectors and coverage metrics (general background knowledge). Deploy conservative, high-precision heuristics to flag sentences that assert facts without proximal evidence anchors. Complement these with simple citation-coverage statistics (e.g., fraction of candidate claims with explicit source pointers) to prioritize human review effort.

- Progressive deployment and component ablations (general background knowledge). Roll out the system in constrained, review-rich settings (internal drafting, closed-domain authoring) and perform ablations that disable one component at a time (graph scheduling, evidence injection, JSON constraints) to isolate their contributions before broader scaling.

Operational recommendations

- Track provenance and versioning (general background knowledge). Persist evidence identifiers, prompt templates, retrieval timestamps, and model checkpoints used for each section so auditors can reproduce or re-run specific outputs.

- Surface uncertainty and failure explanations to users (general background knowledge). Generate explicit, machine-readable uncertainty indicators or “needs citation” flags when evidence is weak or absent; make these flags directly actionable in downstream tooling and review interfaces.

- Prioritize editor tooling (general background knowledge). Provide small UI affordances that let editors accept, edit, or replace evidence citations in-place and trigger revalidation of JSON outputs; such tooling reduces friction and leverages human expertise efficiently.

Concluding remark

The recommendations above are framed conservatively to reduce unsupported assertions and improve auditability. Where prior work directly informs a mitigation (for example, on citation-failure analysis and mitigation strategies), we cite that literature \cite{2510.20303v1}; other recommendations are presented as practical background strategies that merit empirical validation. Given the constrained evaluation resources used in this study, broader claims about the efficacy of individual mitigations should be tested in future work using larger, more diverse corpora and systematic ablation studies.
